newsitem.title: USA: Clinton calls Ross-Arafat talks encouraging.
newsitem.headline: Clinton calls Ross-Arafat talks encouraging.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Thursday said talks between U.S. envoy Dennis Ross and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat aimed at salvaging the Middle East peace process were encouraging.

"Ambassador Ross had a very good meeting with Chairman Arafat and he's proceeding now on his trip. I don't have anything else to tell you but he was encouraged by the response of Chairman Arafat to the matters that we discussed," he told reporters at the White House.

He gave no details and the State Department was also mum about the content of the discussions that Ross had in Rabat, Morocco, with Arafat before flying to Israel for talks with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Meanwhile, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said she would be "deeply involved" in the Middle East peace process and may decide about making a trip to the region herself after Ross returns to Washington. He is expected to report back to Clinton and Albright on Friday or Saturday.

"I will go to the region as it is appropriate as we assess what Dennis is coming back with," she said, referring to Ross' emergency mission to keep the latest crisis from derailing the 6-year-old peace process between Israel and the Palestinians.

"I suspect I will be deeply involved because the issue of the Middle East peace process is one of major national interest to the United States. It is very important as an issue for the United States and obviously for the people in the region," she told a brief news conference at the State Department with Estonian Foreign Minister Toomas Ilves.

Albright, who took office on Jan. 23, has yet to travel to the Middle East, a region her successor Warren Christopher visited more often than any other and whose problems he made the major focus of his tenure. Albright's first overseas trip was to key European and Asian capitals; her second was to the U.S.-Russia summit in Helsinki.

Ross was sent to the region on Wednesday to defuse tensions following a suicide bombing in Tel Aviv last week carried out by Palestinian militants. He wants to get Israel and the Palestinians back into negotiations.

Many Palestinians feel betrayed by Israel's decision to go forward with building new Jewish settlements in Arab East Jerusalem and say this violates Oslo peace accords promises to decide Jerusalem's future in final status negotiations.
On a radio interview programme earlier on Thursday, Albright again repeated the U.S. call for Arafat to give a "red light" to stop violent acts against Israel.

"What we think is that it is very important for Chairman Arafat to give a red light to the terrorist activities," she said, adding that Arafat needed to make a "100 percent effort" to try to halt the violence. While Arafat condemned the bombing, she added, there had to be "no perception that he is in any way allowing terrorist acts to go forward, so we think he needs to give a red light on that."
Albright held separate meetings with Arab-American and Jewish-American leaders on Wednesday and heard strong words from both groups about the crisis in Mideast peacemaking.

Jewish leaders said afterwards they supported Albright in her call for Arafat to make a vigorous statement giving an unambiguous "red light" to anti-Israel attacks. But Arab leaders said Washington had focused unfairly on Arafat and called on the United States to "toughen" its stance and insist that Israel halt plans to build the new Jewish housing.
